headline: Alimbekov Library opens show of 12 manuscript facsimiles; all originals stay put
dek: Entry is free until 31 January, and the Chu Psalter on display is a copy of a book that remains in St Petersburg.
paragraphs: The National Library of Irad, known in Talas as the Alimbekov Library, opened a winter exhibition of twelve facsimile manuscripts and documents on Monday at 14 University Street. It runs to 31 January 2027. Entry is free.

Every item on show is a copy. The library says the originals are not being moved from the institutions that hold them, and that the aim is simpler than a loan show: to let readers see the script and the shape of the page. The IradOne reported the exhibition on Saturday, 21 November, as a free display of twelve facsimiles; the Herald's visit on opening day confirmed the count and the terms.

The copies come from four sources. One group comes from the Talas State University history department's work on Sogdian-Turkic inscriptions in the 1970s and 1980s, a field in which Amanbek Alimbekov, after whom the library is named, was active. A second comes from the Cathedral Seminary Library at Iyık Janyl, which holds the Talas Gospel Lectionary of about 1185 and the 13th-century Gospels of Iyık Janyl, both shown here as facsimiles. A third is the facsimile of the Chu Psalter. A fourth is made up of Persian-language Kokand chancery papers.

The Kokand papers are not photographs. The State Archives of Irad has lent drawn copies from its online exhibition of Kokand charters, and the Archives' director, Mattay Sheraliev, said the distinction matters to visitors. "These are drawn copies, and they show the hand of the chancery clerk," he said. "The papers themselves stay in our fonds, where the reading room can still serve them."

Dr Toma Beishenaliev, the TSU historian, spoke at the opening on the script and on the languages of the valley's trade. He said a reader of the inscriptions meets a country that wrote in several hands at once. "A merchant on the Talas road wrote in Sogdian, spoke Turkic and prayed in Syriac, and the page tells you which was which," he told the audience.

The Chu Psalter is the item with a history attached. It is a 13th-century Christian Turkic Psalter in Syriac script from the Chu valley, bought by a tsarist orientalist expedition in 1881 and held since then in an academic collection in St Petersburg. The archeparchy has asked for its return in 1993, 2007 and 2018, and the ISEZ backed the 2018 request. The Russian answer has been that it was lawfully acquired and belongs to Russia's collections. A full-size facsimile has stood in the seminary library since 2021, and the one in Talas is a second way for readers who cannot travel to Iyık Janyl, about 347 km away by road, to see it. The library's notes do not mention the dispute.

Visitors on Monday included Rustam Aliev, 26, who repairs phones at a counter in Talas and moved from Nurzhan in October. He came for the Syriac pages and admitted he could read none of them. "My Iradi is chala, and this is harder," he said, though he added that the free entry was why he looked in.

A small catalogue is on sale at the TSU Press shop in the university's main building, 12 University Street, where payment is in som and cash only. Those who cannot afford it can still read the wall labels, which carry the holder, the date and the language of each item.
The exhibition closes on 31 January. Nothing in it replaces a visit to the originals, which remain at Iyık Janyl and in the Archives, and, in the Psalter's case, in St Petersburg.
